3.6. Municipalities 
The analyses of municipal divisions amplified the inequalities 
(Fig. 6), showing an even more significant variation in PCU values be­
tween units. Many municipalities had an average PCU score between 3 
and 4 (Fig. 6), and some from the west and north regions concentrated 
on high PCU scores (4 to 5). A high concentration of 2 to 3 PCU score 
municipalities is related to the ranges (Espinhaço, Iron Quadrangle, 
Mantiqueira) in a North-South trend. Cedro do Abaet´e had the lowest 
percentage of area suitable for agriculture (31%) and an average PCU of 
2.25 (standard deviation of 0.40) (Fig. 7 and Table 6 - supplementary 
material). 
4. Discussion 
Global land use has increased considerably in recent decades and 
Brazil is one of the countries with the largest change from native to the 
anthropic area (Winkler et al., 2021). Methodologies aimed at the 
agrosilvopastoral aptitude are necessary for establishing public policies 
that enable sustainable land use (Briassoulis, 2019; Chasek et al., 2019) 
as well as conservation use areas (Ghoddousi et al., 2022; Jiang et al., 
2022). The EZ must be combined with several other components, such as 
legislation, endangered species, tourism interest, etc. Even if a region 
has a high potential for agricultural use, it is essential to have a portion 
of conserved areas for storing reservoirs of native species and for 
providing ecological services like pollination, pest control, water pro­
duction, etc. 
Concerning the PUC environmental factors, Minas Gerais lithology 
shows a predominance of low scores considering PCU, represented by 
gneisses, metapelites, granites (eastern and southwest), quartzite (cen­
tral) slate, siltite (central/ northwestern), and arenite (west) portions. 
The (meta) limestones conditioned the highest weight scores for po­
tential use in the state territory (Costa et al., 2017). The Red Yellow 
Oxisols, Red Oxisols, and Ultisols, widely present in the Minas Gerais, 
conditioned the medium to high PCU due to the advanced weathering 
stage, deep, good drainage conditions, and low cation exchange capacity 
(Bünemann et al., 2018). Entisols, with a low score for potential use, are 
associated with resistant rocks (Taveira et al., 2021), such as quartzites 
and itabirites. The vegetation formed in these shallow and lithic soils has 
high endemism (Schaefer et al., 2016) and must be preserved (Silveira 
et al., 2016; Colli-Silva et al., 2019). The ecological features claim 
protection creating double enforcement for conservation and promoting 
ecosystem services as indicated by the Brazilian law (Brazil, 2021). 
Although Minas Gerais state lithologies present low PCU scores, the 
soil and the slope provide an ideal PCU for developing agrosilvopastoral 
activities in a significant portion of the area. However, low PCU regions 
highlight the importance of studies to understand the ecosystem’s fra­
gilities. They must also be combined with other surface characteristics 
related to the biota or other uses that may lead to other than agricultural 
land destinations. This affirmation aims to enhance the responsible use 
of natural resources, following Brazil’s national and international 
commitments, such as the 2030 Agenda (UN, 2015). Methods aiming at 
agricultural zoning (Minas Gerais, 2021), environmental fragility map­
ping (Ross, 2012; França et al., 2022a), and the potential use evaluation 
(Costa et al., 2017) tend to encourage and promote appropriate agri­
cultural practices in areas with high aptitude. On the other hand, those 
methods should also promote natural vegetation recovery in low po­
tential regions and discourage low potential land for agrosilvopastoral 
use (BPBES, 2019; Brazil, 2021). 
The terrain slope is the main layer, with a high weight (50%) and the 
highest resolution and detail layer in the PCU spatial distribution. The 
slope determines the intensity of processes such as erosion and redis­
tribution of sediments, local drainage capacity, and the amount and 
power of solar radiation (Abate and Kibret, 2016). At regional scales, 
topographic heterogeneity contributes to soil moisture’s spatial het­
erogeneity (Chadwick and Asner, 2016) which can also shape species 
distribution and habitat diversity (Engelbrecht et al., 2007; Comita 
et al., 2009; Jucker et al., 2018). Water availability in tropical soils 
severely limited vegetation growth and productivity (Silva et al., 2013). 
For these reasons, the slope layer defines the transitions and details of 
the PCU. Although the soil type and lithology maps have lower spatial 
resolution than the slope, the PCU calculation can be continuously 
updated and improved as more refined scale maps become available. 
Costa et al. (2019) divided the PCU into five classes regarding the 
potential for conservation use. This work adopted the most straightfor­
ward division for analysing the fitness for use: PCU ≥3 indicated apti­
tude for agrosilvopastoral activities and PCU<3 for biodiversity 
conservation (Table 2). The methodology allows rapid reprocessing 
allowing different divisions readily. Although, we do not ignore the need 
for conservation initiatives inside the productive landscape to ensure 
adequate supplies of pollinators, seed dispersers, herbivores, natural 
enemies, and so on (Nelson and Burchfield, 2021). Moreover, it is also 
necessary to consider conserving the streamflow margins and other 
areas demanded by law (Brazil, 2021). 
We emphasize that other factors such as climate (Gomes et al., 2020), 
the capital and technology applied to land use (Taveira et al., 2021), 
logistic network (Lupinetti-Cunha et al., 2022), and distance to markets 
can also affect the land use potential and were not considered in this 
study. It is essential to have regional studies to develop policies for 
conservation. Levels of agricultural management must be analysed 
considering the land use capability from the different applications of 
capital and technology (Taveira et al., 2021) or even considering the 
roadless and railroad-less opportunity for conservation (Tisler et al., 
2022). Besides restoring degraded areas and mitigating forest degrada­
tion, measures to contain deforestation are necessary to avoid drastic 
loss of biomass and biodiversity (Lima et al., 2020). The challenge to 
land use planning must be the improvement of land use efficiency and 
the reduction of new areas opening. The ecosystem services approach in 
landscape design and accountability may be a great driver to face this 
challenge, especially at the government level (IBGE, 2020b; Agra et al., 
2021). 
4.1. Potential conservation use by administrative, watershed, and 
municipalities divisions 
The administrative divisions have a better balance in terms of agri­
cultural aptitude than the watershed districts and municipal divisions. 
These results highlight the necessity to improve generic programs of 
land use designed for larger scales before implementation in munici­
palities or watershed districts. Despite this apparent balance between 
divisions, a most in-depth analysis becomes recommended since each 
region has climate and logistical differences beyond the methodology 
analysed here. For example, the North and part of Jequitinhonha region 
of the Minas Gerais state, which scored with high PCU, is partly in areas 
susceptible to desertification, classified as semiarid (IBGE, 2018; França 
et al., 2022a). The contrast of the suitable regions and land use for the 
agrosilvopastoral use at the North, Northwest, Mucuri, and Jequitinhonha 
valleys can be conditioned to climate conditions and lower populational 
density from the state (0–25 0–25 inhabitant/km2) compared with the 
Belo Horizonte region (> 500 inhabitant /km2) (IBGE, 2010).

EV_evidence_register.selection_justification: VONT GAP flagged for the team: no canonical variable exists for riparian buffer continuity / gap fraction along the stream network, yet it is the directly mappable 'where is the buffer missing' layer for a zonal_linear product and this source weights it as an MCDA criterion. Raised as a candidate new canonical variable. EV_evidence_register.quote: The ﬁrst example of a top-down approach is Brazil’s 2012 Native Vegetation Protection Law which establishes mandatory restoration of riparian buﬀers across all ecosystems at a national scale (Table 1).
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: national legal mandate requiring riparian buffer restoration (Brazil, 2012 Native Vegetation Protection Law)
EV_evidence_register.attribution: Brazil's 2012 Native Vegetation Protection Law, as reported by Meli et al. (2019)
EV_evidence_register.selection_justification: Routed to operational_risk (M2b Stream-B enabling environment), NOT T4: per the 2026-06-23 re-ratification only HARD, mappable legal masks belong in T4, and this source states the existence of a national restoration mandate WITHOUT any statutory width, so nothing mappable can be derived from it. It is real enabling-environment evidence (a legal driver that makes riparian restoration mandatory at national scale) and feeds M2b / Module-6 next-steps. The companion statutory WIDTHS are captured as structural_suitability from two other sources in this sweep (neotropical_riparian_biodiversity_thresholds_2020, brazil_landuse_loworder_streams_2018).

EV_evidence_register.quote: Inadequate funding at the planning and implementation stages seriously jeopardizes the probability of success, which hinders the de-velopment or implementation of management plans including mon-itoring and enforcement.

EV_evidence_register.selection_justification: Soft, investment-addressable enabling-environment factor -> operational_risk (M2b Stream-B), never T4. Identifies finance as a gating condition for riparian restoration delivery in LMIC rural landscapes. Carries no threshold, so it is emitted as scoping_candidate (variable-selection evidence) with a null relationship rather than a fabricated scale.

relationship.direction: natural regeneration of riparian vegetation is constrained where the floodplain soil seed bank has been depleted by prolonged agricultural occupation and where dispersal of desirable species is limited; such sites require active reintroduction of plant material and topsoil remediation rather than passive restoration
limiting_factors: soil seed bank depletion after decades of agricultural occupation

context.systems: flooded meadows of Central and Northern Europe; riparian swamps (bottomland hardwood forests) of the Southern U.S.

EV_evidence_register.quote: The paucity of the soil seed bank of the ﬂoodplain after decades of human occupation and limited dispersal of desirable species are widely seen as the main con-straints for the recovery of the plant community in European meadows and U.S. swamps (articles 9, 39, 41, 65 and 139 Appendix S1).
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: paucity of floodplain soil seed bank + limited propagule dispersal
EV_evidence_register.attribution: synthesis of articles 9, 39, 41, 65 and 139 of the review's Appendix S1
EV_evidence_register.selection_justification: This is THE dominant limiting factor of the natural_restored family made explicit: whether a degraded riparian site can regenerate without planting depends on residual seed bank and propagule supply, both degraded by prolonged prior agricultural use. It generalises across two continents and many studies (not n=1 site context), and is a suitability/applicability statement rather than an effectiveness result. VONT GAP flagged: no canonical variable yet exists for regeneration potential in riparian systems (the FMNR analogue `rootstock_presence` is NOT interchangeable - seed bank and living rootstock are different mechanisms), so a descriptive id is used and raised for the team. FAMILY NOTE: the claim is generic-riparian (it applies to retained/regenerated and to planted buffers alike); no riparian cross_family id exists, so it is filed under the family the source was discovered and screened under (riparian_buffer__natural_restored), per the 2026-09 sweep brief.

relationship.measured_as: statutory minimum riparian reserve width on EACH side of the watercourse
relationship.direction: required riparian reserve width increases with watercourse width

context.instrument: Native Vegetation Protection Law, Federal Law No. 12,651/2012

EV_evidence_register.quote: In Brazil, the Native Vegetation Protection Law (Federal Law Number 12,651/2012) states that landowners in all biomes must protect a minimum width of ripar-ian reserves. The extent of these riparian reserves varies according to watercourse width (e.g. from 30 m on each side for watercourses up to 10-m wide to 500-m for watercourses larger than 600-m width).
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: statutory minimum width of riparian reserves (Area de Preservacao Permanente) by watercourse width class
EV_evidence_register.attribution: Brazilian Native Vegetation Protection Law, Federal Law No. 12,651/2012 (as reported by Dala-Corte et al. 2020)
EV_evidence_register.selection_justification: Hard legal mask material, which the 2026-06-23 routing keeps INSIDE T4 (only soft, investment-addressable enabling-environment factors go to M2b). The statutory ladder is directly mappable: a distance raster from the stream network, keyed to watercourse width class. Only the two endpoints stated verbatim in the quote are encoded; the intermediate statutory classes are not in this source and are NOT invented. This is a national normative rule, not the study's own site context.

relationship.direction: watercourse size class is the gating variable that selects which riparian reserve width applies

relationship.measured_as: riparian reserve width on EACH side of the stream channel

context.evidence_base: TITAN thresholds over 1,149 fish and 1,449 aquatic-invertebrate stream sites
context.watercourses: small streams up to 10 m wide

EV_evidence_register.quote: Therefore, maintaining 50 m of ripar-ian reserves on each side of the stream channel (resulting in a 100-m wide strip in total) would most effectively avoid crossing thresholds of aquatic biodiversity loss in Brazil.
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: science-based recommended minimum riparian reserve width per side
EV_evidence_register.selection_justification: Extracted as T4 because the authors state it as a SITING/DESIGN REQUIREMENT ('maintaining 50 m of riparian reserves on each side'), which the sweep brief permits for biodiversity width thresholds; the underlying biodiversity DOSE-RESPONSE results (mean thresholds of 6.5% / 2.9% native-vegetation loss, and the per-biome threshold tables) are outcome responses = deferred nbs_effect and are deliberately NOT extracted and NOT relabelled. claim_basis=modelled because the recommendation is derived from the paper's TITAN threshold models. NOTE for synthesis: this science-based minimum is ~1.7x the federal statutory minimum for the same stream class (see ev_distance_to_waterbody_dalacorte20_1) - a genuine, documented divergence.

relationship.direction: sub-national regulations set riparian reserve widths above the federal minimum and scale them with watercourse size

context.municipalities: Bonito (Mato Grosso do Sul); Aparecida de Goiania (Goias)

EV_evidence_register.quote: For example, the city of Bonito (Mato Grosso do Sul State), which relies on ecotourism, has a specific regulation that mandates the protection of 50-m wide riparian reserves around watercourses of rural areas (Bonito, 2004). Aparecida de Goiânia (Goiás State) has also a specific municipal regulation of 50-m wide riparian reserves for small watercourses, and 100 m for other larger rivers (Aparecida de Goiânia, 2018).
EV_evidence_register.attribution: Bonito (2004) municipal law, Mato Grosso do Sul; Aparecida de Goiania (2018) Lei Complementar No. 152, Goias
EV_evidence_register.selection_justification: Worked example of a CONTEXT OVERRIDE for the T4 binding layer: sub-national statutes set riparian widths above the national floor and key them to watercourse size, which is exactly the most-specific-context-wins pattern the recipe encodes via `context_overrides`. Hard legal mask material, so it stays in T4.

EV_evidence_register.quote: The high variability in biodiversity responses to loss of native riparian vegetation suggests caution in the use of a single riparian width for conservation actions or policy definitions nationwide.
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: caution against a single national riparian width
EV_evidence_register.selection_justification: Variable-selection / parameterisation evidence, deliberately carrying NO relationship: it does not set a width, it establishes that a SINGLE global width is not defensible and that riparian width must be context-resolved. Directly supports emitting the T4 riparian-width row with `context_overrides` plus an honest uncertainty band rather than one global number.

EV_evidence_register.quote: In addition, for riparian reserves cleared before 2008, the law allows agricultural activities within them and states that restoration depends on property size (Brancalion et al., 2016). As a consequence, riparian reserves are even smaller in private properties where deforestation occurred before 2008, and watercourse width is not taken into consid-eration in these cases.
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: legal derogation: pre-2008 cleared riparian reserves — restoration obligation scaled by property size
EV_evidence_register.attribution: Brancalion et al. (2016); Brazilian Native Vegetation Protection Law
EV_evidence_register.selection_justification: Enabling-environment / compliance caveat -> operational_risk (M2b Stream-B), not T4. Materially qualifies the T4 statutory mask extracted from the same page: the legally protected riparian width is NOT uniform, because pre-2008 clearing triggers a property-size-dependent derogation in which watercourse width is ignored. Flagged so the mask is not applied more strictly than the law actually binds. No numeric rule is encoded (the derogation's property-size bands are not in this source).

context.instruments: PES, concessional credit, rural land-tax relief

EV_evidence_register.quote: Creating and expanding economic incentives for landowners that protect large riparian reserves can be more effective than tradi-tional command-and-control approaches. Economic incentives may include payment for ecosystem services, access to lower interest rate loans and reduced rural territorial taxes.
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: economic incentives for landowners protecting riparian reserves (PES, lower-interest loans, reduced rural land taxes)
EV_evidence_register.selection_justification: Soft, investment-addressable enabling-environment lever -> operational_risk (M2b Stream-B) and Module-6 next-steps. Relevant because riparian reserves sit on private land (the source notes ~62% of Brazil is privately owned), so finance instruments, not the mask alone, determine whether restoration happens. No threshold, hence scoping_candidate with a null relationship.

relationship.measured_as: riparian zone (Permanent Preservation Area) buffer width measured from the river network
relationship.direction: the riparian zone is delineated as a fixed-width band from the river network, with a wider radial buffer around springs

context.instrument: Native Vegetation Protection Law of Brazil (Brasil, 2012) — Permanent Preservation Area (PPA/APP)
context.corroboration: FAO recommendation and Welsch (1991) give the same 30 m

EV_evidence_register.quote: We adopted the Permanent Preservation Area (PPA) that is deﬁned by the Native Vegetation Protection Law of Brazil (Brasil, 2012) as a riparian zone. We have adopted partially the law and used a 30 m-buﬀer along the river network and a 50 m buﬀer around springs. We did not consider special cases of the law that allow reducing the PPA to only 5 m. FAO recommendation for riparian zone to water quality protection is also 30 m, as well as proposed by Welsch (1991).
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: Permanent Preservation Area (PPA) riparian zone delineation: 30 m river buffer, 50 m spring buffer, 5 m reduced statutory case
EV_evidence_register.observed_dataset: IBGE 1:50,000 stream network + 5 m DEM-derived river network, ArcGIS 10.2
EV_evidence_register.attribution: Native Vegetation Protection Law of Brazil (Brasil, 2012); FAO; Welsch (1991)
EV_evidence_register.selection_justification: The single most directly usable riparian T4 mask rule in this sweep: it gives the statutory delineation geometry (fixed-width band from the river network PLUS a distinct radial buffer around SPRINGS/headwater sources, a spatial feature no other source in the sweep supplies), the reduced statutory case, and an independent FAO corroboration of the same 30 m - all in one contiguous quote. Extracted from a methods section (a section type the catalogue warns about) ONLY because the content is a national statutory + FAO normative rule that generalises, not the study site's own measured conditions; it is therefore not site_context. Encoded as a delineation rule; the paper's water-quality results are deferred nbs_effect and are not extracted.

relationship.direction: published riparian-zone delineation widths span well above the national statutory minimum, and the delineation width chosen changes which scale appears to control the system

context.studies: Tran et al. (2010), USA; Shen et al. (2015), China

EV_evidence_register.quote: The studies which reported that the LULC pattern in the riparian zone plays a greater role than the LULC within the watershed used diﬀerent buﬀer widths. For example, Tran et al. (2010) considered 200 m of riparian zone along the rivers in the USA, while Shen et al. (2015) worked with a buﬀer zone of 100 m in China.

EV_evidence_register.attribution: Tran et al. (2010); Shen et al. (2015)

Useful as an uncertainty/ sensitivity input to the T4 riparian-width row, not as a suitability bound - hence no abs_/opt_ keys.

EV_evidence_register.quote: Low-order streams (1st to 3rd orders) dominate a riverine land-scape, and they contribute to the function, health, and biodiversity of the entire river networks (Vannote et al., 1980; Wipﬂi et al., 2007). Terrestrial inputs strongly inﬂuence low-order streams (Vannote et al., 1980), which make them fragile ecosystems that can suﬀer dramatic impacts of land-use changes.
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: low-order (1st-3rd order) streams as the sensitive target class
EV_evidence_register.attribution: Vannote et al. (1980); Wipfli et al. (2007)
EV_evidence_register.selection_justification: Variable-selection evidence for stream_order as a riparian targeting variable: low-order streams dominate the network and are the most strongly influenced by adjacent terrestrial inputs, so they are where riparian condition matters most. Deliberately emitted WITHOUT shape params: the source defines the low-order class (1st-3rd) but does NOT state a targeting rule of the form 'buffer orders 1-3', and encoding abs_min/abs_max here would be the extractor's inference, not the source's claim.

relationship.direction: low-productivity pasture with low stocking adjacent to watercourses is the preferred land-cover class for riparian forest restoration (low opportunity cost, high restorable area)

EV_evidence_register.quote: According to Latawiec et al. (2015), the low-productivity pas-turelands with few cattle are a great opportunity for forest restoration in the tropical agricultural landscapes.
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: low-productivity pastureland as the restoration opportunity class
EV_evidence_register.selection_justification: System-constraint targeting rule on adjacent land cover: it names the mappable land-cover class where riparian restoration is most feasible in tropical agricultural landscapes, which is the 'constrain by observed distribution' logic applied to the host land-use system. Generalising (stated for tropical agricultural landscapes), not a site observation. No threshold is stated, so `relationship` carries direction and the target class only - no invented scale.

relationship.direction: buffer width requirement is conditioned on slope: on gentle slopes below the stated gradient the stated width range is adequate; steeper ground requires wider buffers

context.context: agricultural riparian buffer strips, diffuse-pollution mitigation

EV_evidence_register.quote: This makes it difficult to derive generic optimum widths, however, for gentle slopes (less than 10 % gradient), widths of 8–15 m are typically adequate (Dorioz et al., 2006).
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: slope gradient (%) as the conditioning factor for adequate buffer strip width
EV_evidence_register.justification_quote: Optimum width depends on site-specific factors (e.g. run-off sediment loads, pollutant type, soil type and slope), vegetation structure (influencing the ability of the vegetation to trap sediments and sediment bound pollutants) and spe-cies composition (influencing assimilation and biodegradation) (Dosskey et al., 2008, 2010; Schmitt et al., 1999).
EV_evidence_register.selection_justification: The only quantified slope rule recovered in this sweep, and the cleanest slope->width design relationship: it conditions the required riparian strip width on slope gradient. Deliberately NOT encoded with abs_min/abs_max on slope - the 10% figure is the BREAKPOINT at which the stated width range ceases to be adequate, NOT a hard slope exclusion, and reading it as one would be the lowest-rank-class-as-exclusion defect. FAMILY: assigned to riparian_buffer__planted because the claim is explicitly about deliberately established vegetated/grass buffer strips in agricultural fields, not about retained or naturally regenerating riparian vegetation.

relationship.direction: a wider riparian strip is required where soluble pollutants (nitrates, dissolved phosphorus) rather than sediment-bound pollutants are the design target

EV_evidence_register.quote: Schmitt et al. (1999) suggested widths of 7.5 m are ef-fective at trapping sediments and sediment-bound pollutants (e.g. non-soluble phosphates), whereas to control soluble pollutants (e.g. nitrates and dissolved phosphorus) widths of 15 m are recommended.
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: recommended buffer strip width by target pollutant transport pathway
EV_evidence_register.justification_quote: Optimum width depends on site-specific factors (e.g. run-off sediment loads, pollutant type, soil type and slope), vegetation structure (influencing the ability of the vegetation to trap sediments and sediment bound pollutants) and spe-cies composition (influencing assimilation and biodegradation) (Dosskey et al., 2008, 2010; Schmitt et al., 1999).
EV_evidence_register.selection_justification: Width PRESCRIPTION (a spatial design rule) rather than an effectiveness measurement: the encoded values are the recommended zone widths, and the underlying removal efficiencies they are meant to achieve are deferred nbs_effect and are not extracted. Same shape as the accepted riparian pilot precedent (slope->required-width rules). FAMILY: riparian_buffer__planted — explicitly established agricultural buffer strips.

relationship.direction: riparian buffer placement should be targeted preferentially at the lowest-order headwater streams, which deliver most of the water and pollutant load to receiving waterbodies

EV_evidence_register.quote: With most of the water entering receiving wa-terbodies via first and second-order headwater streams, targeting ri-parian buffers to protect these streams is particularly important (Correll, 2005).
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: first and second-order headwater streams as the priority targeting class
EV_evidence_register.selection_justification: An explicit stream-order TARGETING rule - the clearest statement in the sweep that riparian buffer placement should be prioritised on the lowest-order headwaters. The orders are written as words in the source, so they are carried as a descriptive `target_class` string and NOT as numeric shape params; inventing numeric bounds the quote does not show would be a smuggled-number defect. Generic riparian placement claim, so it stays with the sweep's discovery family. relationship.direction: steeply sloped riparian banks raise diffuse-pollution risk and call for a WIDER buffer; low-risk, gently sloped extensively managed ground is a low priority and may be left unbuffered

EV_evidence_register.quote: The spatial targeting of riparian buffers should therefore consider the lo-cation of the waterbody in the watershed, in addition to local factors that influence diffuse pollution risk, such as, soil type, slope and sur-rounding land use and management. Wider buffers should be targeted to high risk areas (i.e. intensively managed farms with steeply sloped banks) leaving low risk areas (e.g. areas of extensively managed upland grazing) unbuffered.

relationship.direction: below 10 persons/km2 the landscape supports WIDE-SCALE restoration (single intervention type, incl. assisted or spontaneous natural regeneration and mixed-species plantations); at 10-100 persons/km2 only MOSAIC restoration applies, spatially mixed with agricultural land uses

EV_evidence_register.quote:
Wide-scale restoration opportunities involve
areas with less intensive land use where a single type of interven-
tion is applied (IUCN and WRI 2014). These areas typically have
a population density below 10/km2, and they account for 21 per-
cent of restoration opportunities worldwide (Laestadius et al.
2012). Approaches suitable for wide-scale restoration include
mixed-species plantations or assisted or spontaneous natural rege-
neration. In areas with higher population density (10–100/km2)
and more intensive land use, mosaic restoration opportunities
encompass larger areas and utilize a combination of interventions
that are spatially mixed with agricultural land uses within the lan-
dscape matrix (Fig. 1).
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: local human population density banding of restoration opportunity (wide-scale vs mosaic)
EV_evidence_register.attribution: IUCN and WRI 2014; Laestadius et al. 2012

relationship.direction: for ex-field RWH the requirement SPLITS: the catchment area is best on SHALLOW soils, which shed runoff, while the crop basin that receives it needs DEEP soils — so a single soil-depth layer cannot score the practice, and the source leaves it out of the model

EV_evidence_register.quote:
The soil dataset was not used as a physical attribute in the
XRWH suitability model since good XRWH catchment areas are
those with shallow soils while XRWH crop basins have deep soils.
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: why soil depth is excluded from the ex-field RWH suitability model

classes of order 2, 3, 4, 5 and ≥ 6 are assigned scores 5, 4, 3,

indicates high runoff and low infiltration of water into the 
subsurface (Horton 1945) and then better potential for dam 
location (Rahmati et al. 2019).
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: drainage density as an indicator of check-dam potential

relationship.scale: coefficient in the adoption (selection) equation of an endogenous switching regression; significance stars as reported in the table
relationship.direction: receiving information from an extension agent significantly RAISES the likelihood of adopting bunds — extension reach is an enabling condition for the practice

EV_evidence_register.raw_name: extension contact as an adoption determinant for bunds

relationship.scale: coefficient in the adoption (selection) equation of an endogenous switching regression; significance stars as reported in the table
relationship.direction: access to credit significantly raises bund adoption — finance is an operational lever, not a biophysical constraint

EV_evidence_register.raw_name: credit access as an adoption determinant for bunds

relationship.scale: coefficient in the adoption (selection) equation of an endogenous switching regression; significance stars as reported in the table
relationship.direction: larger total rice area raises the likelihood of adopting bunds, but only weakly significant - the weakest of the three enabling factors here

EV_evidence_register.raw_name: farm size as an adoption determinant for bunds

relationship.direction: slopes above 75% are generally unsuitable for planting because seedlings are hard to establish there — an upper bound for active planting

EV_evidence_register.quote:
Areas with slopes greater than 75% are generally unsuitable for 
planting due to establishment difficulties (Santos et al., 2018).

relationship.direction: natural-regeneration potential RISES with local forest density within a 1 km radius and falls with distance to existing forest — surrounding forest is the seed and disperser supply, so this is the landscape's cover, not the site's

EV_evidence_register.quote:
The potential for natural regeneration was positively associated 
with local forest density within a 1 km radius and negatively associ-
ated with distance to existing forest (Fig. 3a,b).
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: local forest density within a 1 km radius as a positive driver of natural regeneration potential

relationship.direction: protected areas are a HARD exclusion from the afforestation/reforestation opportunity space — a legal mask, not a scored factor

EV_evidence_register.quote:
Fig. 2. Global map of CDM-AR suitable land (dark green) within Non-Annex I countries (light yellow), as delineated by the land suitability analysis. A 30%
crown cover density threshold was used to deﬁne forest, and protected areas are not included.
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: protected areas excluded from CDM-AR suitable land

relationship.direction: in Para, Brazil, secondary vegetation may be LEGALLY CLEARED below 10 m2/ha basal area (municipalities >50% primary forest) or below 5 m2/ha (<50%) — young regrowth under the threshold has no legal protection, so passive regeneration is at clearing risk until it crosses it

EV_evidence_register.quote:
For example, in the state of
Para, Brazil, secondary vegetation can be legally cleared if below
10 m2/ha of tree basal area for municipalities with more than 50
percent primary forest or if below 5 m2/ha for those with <50
percent primary forest cover (Vieira et al. 2014).
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: legal basal-area threshold below which secondary vegetation may be cleared

relationship.direction: natural regeneration is not cost-free: stewards need compensating for fencing, fire protection and hunting patrols — the practice depends on a finance mechanism even though it needs no planting

EV_evidence_register.quote:
Natural
regeneration stewards would need to be compensated for costs
of fencing, ﬁre protection, hunting patrols, or other actions that
are needed to promote and sustain naturally regenerating forests
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: compensation of regeneration stewards for protection costs

relationship.direction: for created and restored wetlands, VERY suitable land lies within about 500 m of a frequently flowing stream; cost and energy rise in buffer steps beyond it (the paper's one-hundred-and-fifty-metre buffers), and land above the highest point where water flows frequently is unsuitable without pumping

EV_evidence_register.quote:
Water availability is a critical factor in selecting wetland location. The distance
from frequently flowing streams has a strong influence on the total cost of the
wetland restoration or creation project. Very suitable areas were considered those
within ∼500 m from a frequently flowing stream. Long distances imply high energy
requirements and financial expenditures. Buffers of one hundred and fifty meters
radius were considered as the spatial units that noticeably increase energy and
economical costs. We considered unsuitable for wetland mitigation all catchment
areas located above the highest point where water flowed frequently. In these areas,
only water pumping could keep water on the wet
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: distance from frequently flowing streams as the water-availability criterion

relationship.weight_scale: 1.5 is the maximum layer weight in the model
relationship.direction: calibration settled the low-cost distance at 450 m and gave distance to frequently flowing streams the maximum weight (1.5) — water availability is the most determinant condition under semi-arid conditions

EV_evidence_register.quote:
Water availability was the most determinant condition for a site to be selected
by the model under semi-arid conditions and the highest weight (1.5) was assigned
to the distance to frequently flowing streams layer. Only the maximum value (1.5)
provided enough enhancement of the parameter in selecting places were water was
available at distances with low implementation cost (established at 450 m).
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: calibrated low-cost distance to frequently flowing streams and its model weight

relationship.direction: slope is RESTRICTIVE for wetland creation: the lower the slope, the less earthwork and the cheaper the project — flat land is favoured on construction-cost grounds

EV_evidence_register.quote:
Slope is a restrictive factor in wetland construction and restoration. The main
design considerations and construction budgets rely on it. The lower the slope,
the cheaper the construction project, as a consequence of the smaller amount
of earthwork needed. Extensive earthwork also involves higher energy expenses.
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: slope as a restrictive construction-cost factor for created wetlands

relationship.direction: in semi-arid agricultural catchments the MOST suitable land for new wetlands is irrigated farmland, where frequent watering favours flooding; low-activity land (abandoned, fallow, rain-fed) is also suitable

EV_evidence_register.quote:
Existing land-use is important in determining the suitability of an area for the
establishment of wetlands. The most suitable areas in this semi-arid territory would
be those affected by irrigation, where frequent watering favours wetland flooding.
Areas with low human activity (abandoned, fallow or rain-fed farmlands) are also
suit
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: existing land use classes suitable for wetland establishment

excluded_classes: developed land (open space, low, medium and high intensity)
relationship.direction: restored/new wetlands may only be placed on the remaining land-cover classes; the listed classes are hard exclusions in the placement model

EV_evidence_register.quote:
No placement of new/
restored wetlands was allowed in any of the simulations in areas with 
the following land cover designations: (1) open water; (2) developed 
land (open space, low intensity, medium intensity, high intensity); (3) 
barren land; (4) shrubland; and (5) wetland.

included_classes: low forest cover or non-forested land (reforestation target)
relationship.direction: planting targets are defined as currently non-forested or low-forest-cover land, identified from forest-loss, impervious-surface and land-cover products

EV_evidence_register.quote:
In this study, adjustments were made to the definitions of target 
areas for afforestation and reforestation based on the regulations set by 
the UNFCCC and Ministry of Forestry (MoFE 2015). Afforested areas 
were defined as non-forested regions of > 50 years. However, owing to 
data limitations, an adjusted approach was adopted in which the target 
areas for afforestation were identified by integrating non-forested 
regional information defined as of 2000. This information was sourced 
from Global Forest Watch data (Hansen et al., 2013), integrated with 
impervious surface data from 1983 to 2000 (Gong et al., 2020), and 
MODIS land-cover data since 2000 (USGS, 2010). Consequently, the 
targeted reforestation areas in this study focused on regions with low 
forest cover or non-forested areas observed from 2000 to 2023.
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: non-forested / low forest cover target areas

relationship.direction: tied ridging performs best on coarser-textured soils in the semi-arid site; on clay (fine-textured) soils ridge tillage can induce waterlogging followed by mass movement and erosion - a negative on heavy clays

EV_evidence_register.quote:
The best CEM techniques were diﬀerent for both sites. In Mbeere
South, tied ridging was the best followed by mulching practice while in
Meru South mulching was the best. The tied ridges in the semi-arid site
were hardly destroyed during the cropping season leading to increased
water content in the soil proﬁle and good crop performance while in the
sub-humid site the ridges were repaired often. On clay soils (in Meru
South), ridge tillage can induce water logging, and later on followed by
mass movement/soil erosion (FAO, 1993). Mulching retained more soil
water content in Meru South since the region received more rainfall
compared with Mbeere South. In addition, soils in Meru South are ﬁne
textured, clay while Mbeere South the soils are coarser. Reduced soil
water retention is observed in coarse textured (Mbeere South) than in
ﬁne-textured soils

A trapezoidal bund consists of a base bund, connected to two side bunds at an angle of about 135° and a distance between the tips of 10 – 100 m. Overflow is discharged around the tips of the side bunds. The wings of the side bunds are pref- erably reinforced with stones. Often they are constructed using machinery. Enclosed areas can reach 1 ha in size (C:A 15:1 – 100:1). The technology is suitable for areas with 200 – 400 mm of annual rainfall.

Cultivated reservoirs / tanks are above ground earthen water retention struc- tures. Tanks are constructed on gentile slopes (1 – 10%) by excavating soil and/or building bunds (reservoirs). In this system collected water is either directed from the tank to lower fields or into a below ground tank or shallow well for irrigation (C:A ratio 10:1 – 100:1). When the water of the reservoir is used, the reservoir itself is cropped on soil residual moisture. This system is suitable for areas with 150 – 600 mm annual rainfall.

relationship.direction: small earth/stone storage dams suit semi-arid rainfall

The reservoirs have neither plastered walls nor covered surfaces. The water is mostly used communally for livestock consumption, and for supplementary irrigation. Ndivas are suitable suitable for areas with 300 – 600 mm of rainfall.

They are applied on sloping land (1-20%), however are com- monly found on slopes of 1-5% in areas of 150-500 mm/y of rainfall.

Meskat is rectangular shaped runoff basin. It consists of a catchment area called meskat of about 500 m² in size, and a cropping area called mankaa of about 250 m² (C:A ratio of 2:1). The entire system is surrounded by an approximately 20 cm high bund, and provided with spillways to allow runoff to flow into the mankaa. A meskat can have more than one mankaa arranged in series (see figure below). Surplus runoff spills over one mankaa to the other. Meskats are suitable on slopes of 2-15% and for areas with an annual rainfall of 200 – 400 mm.

relationship.outcome_raw: fuel loads and potential wildfire risk

legacy.qualifier: silvopasture reduces grass biomass, litter, and duff depth, thereby reducing fuel loads and wildfire risk; measured at two Washington State ponderosa pine sites

context.note: migrated v1.5.0→v1.6.0 2026-09-30 (deterministic re-shape, method §10); risk_role=livelihood_mitigation; mitigation_potential=moderate; aez temperate_europe removed 2026-10-02 (US study; T7 has no North-American AEZ id) | comparator=unmanaged_state (Pete 2026-10-19, hazard_cell_comparator): the study compares silvopasture with NON-GRAZED managed forest, not with the open pasture a T3 agro-pastoral cell asks about — informs the account, never sets the class

EV_evidence_register.quote: This study compared forest composition and structure, fuel types, and vegetative biomass between silvopasture and non-grazed managed forests in Washington, U.S. We show that silvopasture management results in reductions in grass biomass, litter, and duff depth when compared to non-grazed managed forest. These findings point to the integrated nature of silvopasture, where management of overstory composition and structure, understory vegetation, and grazing can reduce fuel loads and potential wildfire risk.
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: fuel loads and potential wildfire risk
EV_evidence_register.attribution: Temperate-US scope (Washington State dryland ponderosa pine forest); Mediterranean studies referenced but not the primary site. Findings may not transfer directly to tropical/subtropical or humid-temperate silvopastoral systems.

legacy.qualifier: potential (not measured) reduction in fire frequency — reduced overstory density and spatial variability vs other land uses; epistemic claim only

EV_evidence_register.quote: The reduced density and increased spatial variability of the overstory, combined with other silvopasture management practices, has the potential of reducing fire frequency when compared to other land uses.
EV_evidence_register.attribution: [reviewed 2026-08-06 by Namita-J; reason:confirmed_pass] [reviewed 2026-07-15 by Namita-J; reason:confirmed_pass] [reviewed 2026-07-02 by Namita-J; reason:confirmed_pass] [reviewed 2026-06-30 by Namita-J] Temperate-US paper; claim cites Mediterranean/other research (ref 32). Mechanism is overstory structure management.

legacy.qualifier: rotational grazing removes understory biomass, reducing herbaceous surface fuel loads

context.note: migrated v1.5.0→v1.6.0 2026-09-30 (deterministic re-shape, method §10); risk_role=livelihood_mitigation; mitigation_potential=moderate; aez temperate_europe removed 2026-10-02 (US study; T7 has no North-American AEZ id) | comparator=unmanaged_state (Pete 2026-10-19, hazard_cell_comparator): the study compares silvopasture with NON-GRAZED managed forest, not with the open pasture a T3 agro-pastoral cell asks about — informs the account, never sets the class

EV_evidence_register.quote: For livestock, use of rotational grazing in a silvopasture has been found to effectively remove understory biomass, thus reducing herbaceous surface fuel loads.
EV_evidence_register.attribution: Temperate-US paper; claim cites Mediterranean silvopasture research (refs 28, 33). Mechanism: rotational grazing forage consumption.

relationship.outcome_raw: litter and duff depth

legacy.qualifier: litter and duff depth significantly lower in silvopasture vs non-grazed managed forest at both Washington State study sites (statistical significance reported but p-value not quoted)

EV_evidence_register.quote: Litter and duff depth were significantly lower at both silvopasture sites than the non-grazed managed forests (Table 4). One contributing factor may be due to the significant reduction of grass biomass from livestock grazing at silvopasture sites when compared to non-grazed managed forest sites (Table 5).
EV_evidence_register.attribution: [VERIFY-FLAG mismatch: qualifier states p<=0.05 but the quote only says "significantly lower" — no p-value is stated in the quoted text; this numeric precision is fabricated.] Primary measured data from two Washington State ponderosa pine silvopasture sites; temperate-US scope. Statistical significance at p<=0.05.

context.note: cited model result; study location not stated in passage; retained treed buffers after timber harvest

EV_evidence_register.quote: As an example, Wong and McCuen (1982) modeled the impacts of substrate characteristics, slope, vegetation roughness, and overland ﬂow patterns and suggested that under most circumstances, buffers less than 60 m were sufﬁcient to control sedimentation.

relationship.outcome_raw: 30 m buffers did not prevent stream sedimentation increase after partial clearcutting

context.note: null finding; retained forest buffer after timber harvest

EV_evidence_register.quote: Moring (1982) reported that 30 m buffers were unable to prevent increases in stream sedimentation after a partial clearcutting of small watersheds in Oregon.

relationship.outcome_raw: 9 m strips sufficient to remove sediments from cutblock features

context.note: retained forest strip after timber harvest

EV_evidence_register.quote: In contrast, Haupt and Kidd (1965) found that 9 m strips were sufﬁcient to remove sediments from cutblock features in Rocky Mountain areas of central Idaho.

relationship.outcome_raw: increase in stream temperature after harvest, buffered vs unbuffered (review)

context.note: cited review; intact or partially harvested buffers

EV_evidence_register.quote: In a review of forest practices, Binkley and Brown (1993) noted that almost universal use of intact or partially harvested buffers had signiﬁcantly reduced increases in stream temperature after harvesting.

relationship.outcome_raw: modelled prevention of stream temperature rise by sufficiently wide buffers

context.note: solar-radiation buffer models; location not stated

EV_evidence_register.quote: A number of models exist for prescribing buffer widths to control solar radiation (Beschta and Weatherred, 1984). The important variables include: stream width and volume, buffer forest height and density, amount of watershed cut, solar inputs, and groundwater temperatures. These models suggest that buffers .30 m wide are sufﬁcient to prevent steam temperatures from rising.

relationship.outcome_raw: partially cut 10-20 m buffers still shaded streams and prevented temperature increase

context.note: location not stated in passage

EV_evidence_register.quote: Aubertin and Patric (1974) found that partially cut (,50% retention) buffers (10–20 m wide) were still able to sufﬁciently shade streams and prevent temperature increases.

relationship.outcome_raw: invertebrate community: no harvest impact with buffers >=30 m; diversity change with narrower buffers

EV_evidence_register.quote: Newbold et al. (1980) studied the impact of varying stream buffer widths on invertebrate communities in northern California streams. Streams with buffers $30 m exhibited no impact of harvest on invertebrates, while streams with buffers ,30 m experienced changes in species diversity. For the narrower buffers, the changes in diversity were positively correlated to buffer width.

relationship.outcome_raw: cutthroat trout density recovered after riparian revegetation by shrubs and trees (vs harvest to stream margin)

context.note: location not stated in passage; effect of natural riparian revegetation after harvest to streamside

EV_evidence_register.quote: Young et al. (1999) found that non-anadromous cutthroat trout streams harvested to streamside margins reached a maximum summer temperature of 30 8C, which was correlated with a four-fold decline in ﬁsh density. Fish populations recovered after stream temperatures decreased following revegetation by shrubs and trees.

EV_evidence_register.quote: Out of seven studies conducted on erosion control, 49 observa- tions were identified for runoff and 49 for soil loss. The studies were conducted in Kenya, Nigeria, and Zimbabwe. Our findings show that agroforestry performed best in terms of erosion reduc- tion ecosystem services, five and ten times better than controls for runoff (RR: 5.0; 95% CI: 3.3-7.9) and soil loss (RR: 9.7; 95% CI: 5.9-17.3). However, these very large effect sizes could also be due to publication bias as demonstrated by the high Kendall’s rank correlation coefficients. If we had found more published studies (larger sample sizes), we expect the effect sizes to be more modest than the figures we reported here. Erosion control with agroforestry was more effective in both humid (RR 7.2; 95% CI 4.8 to 13.9) and semi-arid zones (RR 8.0; 95% CI 4.8 to 16.7) compared to controls. Similarly, erosion control with agroforestry was more effective when either shrubs (RR 6.9; 95% CI 4.6 to 11.4) or trees (RR 11.1; 95% CI 6.1 to 24.7) were planted.

context.note: Headline pooled result. 17 studies, 69 RR values (stated on p13). Pantropical humid/sub-humid meta-analysis of agroforestry vs crop monoculture. PICOS note: silvopastoral systems, rotational woodlots and home-gardens were EXPLICITLY EXCLUDED by the authors (p11), so these results do not cover those families. Simultaneous (alley cropping, intercropping, shaded coffee/cocoa) and sequential (improved fallow) practices only; the paper's subgroup split is simultaneous vs sequential, which does not map 1:1 onto FAM families, hence cross_family.

EV_evidence_register.quote: agroforestry compared to the corresponding crop monocultures. Overall, agroforestry trees reduced soil 253 erosion by 50% (Figure 2a). All the studies on soil erosion were conducted in simultaneous agroforestry, 254 and only one study was found on sequential systems. Although the differences were not statistically 255 significant (Figure 2b), tree species that do not fix N generally contributed to lower erosion (RR = 0.29) 256 than N-fixing trees (RR = 0.41).

relationship.outcome_raw: agroforestry systems in East Africa stock an average of 24.2 +/- 2.8 Mg C per ha in biomass

context.note: Pooled mean +/- SE (2.8). Systematic review of 185 East-African publications (livelihoods n = 152, carbon n = 43). NOTE: these are carbon STOCKS (Mg C per ha), not sequestration RATES — a rate requires a time denominator the review does not give.

EV_evidence_register.quote: This review shows that agroforestry systems in East Africa stock an average of 24.2 ± 2.8 Mg C ha−1 in biomass and 98.8 ± 12.2 Mg C ha−1 in the soil (Fig. 3). The combined estimate of carbon in biomass and the soil is larger than what was estimated to be the potential carbon storage (29–53 Mg C ha−1) of agrosilvicultural systems in the humid tropics of Africa (Albrecht and Kandji, 2003), but lower than systems with high stem density, large mean tree size, and longer maximum ages i.e. over 60 years reported in Southeast Asia (Roshetko et al., 2007). The difference with earlier estimates is mostly in the soil part where several method­ ological issues need to be considered (Hairiah et al., 2020), such as variation in the soil depth included and changes in soil bulk density that influence which soil is included in a fixed-depth sample (Schrumpf et al., 2011). The amount varies depending on agroforestry practice, ranging from 26.7 ± 7.0 Mg C ha−1 in improved fallows to 153±23 Mg C ha−1 in homegardens.
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: biomass carbon stock in agroforestry systems

EV_evidence_register.quote: The meta-analysis showed that the effect of SPS on biodiversity compared to their references varied with system types and taxonomic groups. SPS supported 28.4% higher biodiversity than open pastures. SPS with native (unplanted) and planted trees both increased biodiversity relative to open pastures by 36.3% and 20.9%, respectively. However, SPS with native trees had 18.1% lower biodiversity than native forests.
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: biodiversity in SPS vs references (abstract synthesis)

relationship.outcome_raw: in the majority of cases (52%) tree presence had a net positive (47%) or neutral (5%) effect on food yields or yield proxies; regionally, positive effects were reported in 58% (Americas) and 54% (Asia) of studies while a further statement reports 48% of studies in one region recording DECREASED yields

context.note: HEADLINE. QUEUE/SOURCE CAVEAT: the regional sentence names 'Asia' twice with opposite signs — an apparent typo in the published text (the 48%-decrease region is almost certainly Africa per the later regional breakdown 33%/48%/33%). Not resolvable from the text, so no regional unit emitted from this sentence. VOTE-COUNT review: percentages are shares of STUDIES reporting a direction, not effect magnitudes, so metric = narrative. PICOS: 58 of the 74 reviewed studies are agroforestry studies and 53 of those are trees INTRODUCED TO THE FARM (typically alley cropping); only 12 studies concern off-farm natural forest patches. The pooled vote-counts are therefore dominated by, but not exclusive to, agroforestry — read as agroforestry-weighted, not agroforestry-pure.

EV_evidence_register.quote: The overall trend across the studies shows that in the majority of cases (52%) there was a net positive (47%) or neutral (5%) effect of tree presence on food yields or food yield proxies. However, when the results are disaggregated by region, there is a degree of variability (Fig. 5). For example, in the Americas and Asia, tree presence was more likely to enhance food yields with positive effects of trees on yields reported in 58% and 54% of studies for these regions respectively; while in Asia the opposite is the case, with the majority of studies (48%) reporting decreased food yields as a result of tree presence (Fig. 5).
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: effect of tree presence on food yields

relationship.outcome_raw: negative effects of trees on crop yields reported in 33% (Africa), 48% (Asia) and 33% (Americas) of studies, but negative effects on OVERALL LIVELIHOOD outcomes in only 15%, 24% and 8% respectively

context.note: THE UNSUITABLE TAIL: a third to a half of studies record yield LOSSES from tree presence. Asia carries the largest yield penalty. EV_evidence_register.quote: Une méta-analyse rapporte également que le F. albida favoriserait une augmentation moyenne de rendement de respectivement 150 pour cent et 73 pour cent pour le maïs et le sorgho cultivés sous couvert (Ngom et al., 2015). (English: A meta-analysis also reports that F. albida would favour a mean yield increase of 150 per cent and 73 per cent respectively for maize and sorghum grown under the canopy (Ngom et al., 2015).)
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: augmentation moyenne de rendement maïs / sorgho

relationship.outcome_raw: groundnut under F. albida behaves variably: a significant pod-yield rise in one study, variable yields in another, yield decreases in a third

context.note: disagreement within the same tree species; negative arm retained (contract E6)

EV_evidence_register.quote: L’arachide cultivée sous la canopée des F. albida semble avoir un comportement plus variable. Au Sénégal, Dancette et Poulain (1968) ont observé une hausse significative du rendement en gousses (Roupsard et al., 2020), l’Institut de recherche pour les huiles et les oléagineux (1966, cité dans Boffa, 2000) a fait état de rendements variables, alors que Louppe (1996) a plutôt rapporté des baisses de rendement de l’arachide sous le couvert de cette espèce. (English: Groundnut grown under the canopy of F. albida seems to behave more variably. In Senegal, Dancette and Poulain (1968) observed a significant increase in pod yield (Roupsard et al., 2020), the Institute for Research on Oils and Oilseeds (1966, cited in Boffa, 2000) reported variable yields, while Louppe (1996) instead reported yield decreases for groundnut under the cover of this species.)
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: rendement de l'arachide sous couvert de F. albida

relationship.outcome_raw: yield decrease for groundnut and millet grown under Cordyla pinnata canopy compared with outside the cover

context.note: species-dependent depressive effect; pruning reported to limit it

EV_evidence_register.quote: L’impact du C. pinnata sur les rendements a été beaucoup moins étudié, mais les travaux de Samba (1997) font état d’une baisse de rendement des cultures d’arachide et de mil cultivés sous couvert par rapport aux zones hors couvert (Samba, 1997). (English: The impact of C. pinnata on yields has been much less studied, but the work of Samba (1997) reports a yield decrease for groundnut and millet grown under the cover compared with areas outside the cover (Samba, 1997).)
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: rendement arachide et mil sous C. pinnata

relationship.outcome_raw: windbreak hedges have a major impact on wind and play an important role protecting soils from wind erosion on sandy, degraded-cover soils

EV_evidence_register.quote: Elles ont d’abord évidemment un impact majeur sur les vents et jouent un rôle important dans la protection des sols contre l’érosion éolienne, en particulier dans les zones où les sols sont à dominance sableuse et où le couvert végétal est fortement dégradé. (English: They first of all obviously have a major impact on winds and play an important role in protecting soils against wind erosion, particularly in areas where soils are predominantly sandy and where vegetation cover is heavily degraded.)
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: protection des sols contre l'érosion éolienne

relationship.outcome_raw: 23% total yield increase across protected plots in the off-season, despite yield losses within 10 m of the hedge during the rainy season

context.region: perimetres irrigues villageois, vallee du fleuve Senegal

EV_evidence_register.quote: Ainsi, si des baisses de rendement ont été rapportées dans les périmètres irrigués villageois de la vallée du fleuve Sénégal, à une distance allant jusqu’à 10 mètres des haies durant l’hivernage, une hausse totale des rendements de 23 pour cent a été observée dans l’ensemble des parcelles protégées au cours de la contre-saison (English: Thus, while yield decreases have been reported in the village irrigated perimeters of the Senegal River valley, at a distance of up to 10 metres from the hedges during the rainy season, a total yield increase of 23 per cent was observed across all the protected plots during the off-season)
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: rendement des parcelles protégées par haie brise-vent

relationship.outcome_raw: windbreak hedges have a neutral effect on groundnut yield at Bambey

EV_evidence_register.raw_name: effet des haies brise-vent sur le rendement de l'arachide

relationship.outcome_raw: internal rate of return of a windbreak hedge in irrigated rice 36%, rising to 58% when woody products of the hedge are counted

EV_evidence_register.quote: Fall et al. (English: Fall et al. (2002) thus estimated that in the Senegal River valley the internal rate of return of a windbreak hedge in irrigated rice crops was 36 per cent, or even 58 per cent when the contribution of the woody products generated by the hedge was taken into account (Satin, 1998).)
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: taux de rentabilité interne d'une haie brise-vent

relationship.outcome_raw: windbreak hedges generally cause a slight RISE in temperature in the protected plots, with variable impacts by crop and growth stage

(English: Windbreak hedges would moreover generally cause a slight rise in temperatures in the protected plots, which can have variable impacts depending on the crops and their stage of development.)
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: hausse des températures dans les parcelles protégées

relationship.outcome_raw: no clear consensus on windbreak effects during drought: some studies find higher yields in drier years, others find harm to rainfed crops

context.note: explicit disagreement statement - feeds the IPCC agreement axis

EV_evidence_register.quote: La littérature scientifique ne rapporte en outre pas de consensus clair quant aux effets que les haies brise-vent engendrent en période de sécheresse. Certaines études pointent le fait que le rendement de plusieurs cultures établies à proximité de haies brise-vent serait accru durant les années plus sèches (Kanzler et al., 2018; Nuberg, 1998; Thevathasan et Gordon, 2004), tandis que d’autres jugent que l’effet des haies pourrait alors nuire aux cultures non irriguées (FAO, 1986). (English: The scientific literature moreover reports no clear consensus as to the effects that windbreak hedges produce during periods of drought. Some studies point out that the yield of several crops established near windbreak hedges would be increased during drier years (Kanzler et al., 2018; Nuberg, 1998; Thevathasan and Gordon, 2004), while others judge that the effect of the hedges could then harm non-irrigated crops (FAO, 1986).)
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: effets des haies brise-vent en période de sécheresse

relationship.outcome_raw: shade trees reduce sheet erosion by a factor of 2 versus full-sun plots, and raise N2 fixation and N recycling

(English: Compared with full-sun plots, we show that they reduce sheet erosion by a factor of 2, increase atmospheric nitrogen (N2) fixation and the percentage of nitrogen recycled in the system, thus reducing fertiliser requirements.)

EV_evidence_register.quote: Le bilan de carbone a été mesuré par Eddy-covariance des parcelles agroforestières (arbres + caféier + litière + sol) de la ferme d’Aquiares pendant huit années, pour un stockage moyen de 3,6 t C/ha/an. EV_evidence_register.raw_name: bilan de carbone des parcelles agroforestières

relationship.outcome_raw: yield-carbon trade-off: high cocoa yield (>1.5 t/ha) only possible below 100-150 t C/ha of carbon storage

context.note: trade-off curve across 71 inventoried cocoa agroforests

EV_evidence_register.quote: Ainsi, l’obtention d’un rendement élevé (> 1,5 t/ha) n’est possible que pour un niveau de stockage en carbone inférieur à 100-150 t C/ha. À contrario, un niveau de stockage supérieur à 150 t C/ha ne semble pas être compatible avec un rendement accessible supérieur à 750 kg/ha de cacao marchand. (English: Thus, obtaining a high yield (> 1.5 t/ha) is only possible for a carbon storage level below 100-150 t C/ha. Conversely, a storage level above 150 t C/ha does not appear compatible with an attainable yield above 750 kg/ha of marketable cocoa.)
EV_evidence_register.raw_name: compromis rendement cacao / stockage de carbone

relationship.outcome_raw: yield-biodiversity trade-off: >1 t/ha cocoa not attainable above 10 associated species; 750 kg/ha attainable up to 20-23 species

(English: Yields above 1 t/ha of marketable cocoa do not seem attainable for a number of associated species above 10. EV_evidence_register.raw_name: compromis rendement cacao / richesse spécifique associée

Finally, it increases the relative humidity of the air and the soil moisture under the canopy (Avelino et al., 2011).)

3.6 
Market-oriented agroforestry interventions (for example, Acacia decurrens) that 
bring sustainable income for smallholders can be vital ingredients in creating incentives 
for the adoption of biological measures for land restoration and improving resilience to 
climate shocks. Agroforestry systems, such as Acacia decurrens, that bring additional 
benefits through nitrogen fixation while also generating cash income are vital win-win 
options for land restoration, income growth, and asset creation. The lesson is that in the 
microwatersheds where such market-oriented agroforestry practices have been

transformational changes in restoring highly degraded landscapes, creating 
employment, generating income, and reducing poverty and out-migration.

EV_evidence_register.quote:
72. Contribution to climate resilience. Results of a World Bank study suggest that well-established SPS could help 
reduce vulnerability to climate shocks.47 While extensive CR operations in Colombia reported milk productivity losses 
of up to 19 percent during periods of climate variability from 2009 to 2019, farms with well-established SPS reported 
productivity losses of just 0.4-5.5 percent. Under a scenario where SPS are implemented at scale, projections suggest 
producers could avoid annual losses from climate variability equivalent to 680-2,268M liters of milk and 60,000 tons 
of beef. Unlike traditional, extensive systems, well-established SPS are better adapted to climate shocks because their 
improved vegetative cover and efficient land management reduce vulnerability.

relationship.outcome_raw: silvopastoral establishment and maintenance need more skilled labour, more elaborate infrastructure and many more management decisions than pure grass pasture

EV_evidence_register.quote: No caso específico dos SSPs, as estratégias de implantação e manutenção requereriam mão-de-obra mais capacitada (e.g., para o plantio de mudas, poda das árvores, etc.), infra-estrutura mais elaborada (e.g., para o produção de mudas) e, principalmente, maior número de decisões de manejo, quando comparados a sistemas mais tradicionais e menos intensivos de uso da terra, como as pastagens puras de gramíneas. (English: In the specific case of silvopastoral systems, establishment and maintenance strategies would require more skilled labour (e.g. for planting seedlings, pruning the trees, etc.), more elaborate infrastructure (e.g. for seedling production) and, above all, a greater number of management decisions, when compared with more traditional and less intensive land-use systems such as pure grass pastures.)

relationship.outcome_raw: cultural barrier: unfounded belief that shading livestock reduces meat or milk output by cutting grazing time

EV_evidence_register.quote: Ademais, em função do desconhecimento e da falta de informações confiáveis, certas dúvidas e mitos ainda persistem no meio rural com relação aos SSPs, levando a certa aversão ao uso desses sistemas. Por exemplo, existe a crença, cientificamente infundada, por parte de alguns produtores, de que o provimento de sombra aos animais na pastagem poderia diminuir a produção de carne ou leite. A justificativa para isso seria que o acesso voluntário à sombra reduziria o tempo de pastejo (i.e., aumentaria o tempo dedicado ao ócio) e, conseqüentemente, o consumo de forragem. (English: Moreover, because of a lack of knowledge and of reliable information, certain doubts and myths still persist in rural areas regarding silvopastoral systems, leading to a certain aversion to using these systems. For example, there is a scientifically unfounded belief among some producers that providing shade to animals in the pasture could reduce meat or milk production. The justification for this would be that voluntary access to shade would reduce grazing time (i.e. increase idle time) and consequently forage intake.)

(English: The review and meta-analysis showed that, although agroforestry systems present advantages for increased income and environmental recovery, lack of information becomes one of the main barriers to the adoption of agroforestry systems. relationship.outcome_raw: in West Africa planting a tree signifies land tenure, so tenants are legally not allowed to plant trees or establish live fences

context.note: tenure barrier specific to linear/boundary practices

EV_evidence_register.quote: En África Occidental se generan conflictos de intereses por la implantación de cercas vivas, dado que plantar un árbol tiene significado de tenencia de tierra y alinderación de propiedad. Este conflicto afecta directamente la plantación de cercas vivas ya que, por cuestión legal no se permite a los arrendatarios plantar árboles ni mucho menos establecer cercas vivas, ya que esto podría traer problemas legales al momento de heredar. Por lo tanto, en la mayoría de los casos las cercas vivas no surgirían y tendrían que implementar métodos alternos como el caso de cercas muertas (Levasseur et al., 2004). (English: In West Africa conflicts of interest are generated by the establishment of live fences, since planting a tree has the meaning of land tenure and property demarcation. This conflict directly affects the planting of live fences since, for legal reasons, tenants are not allowed to plant trees, let alone establish live fences, as this could bring legal problems at the time of inheritance. Therefore, in most cases live fences would not arise and they would have to implement alternative methods such as dead fences (Levasseur et al., 2004).)

EV_evidence_register.quote: Entre los once estudios que midieron la escorrentía en 52 parcelas, todos mostraron una reducción en la escorrentía como resultado de las zanjas de infiltración. El análisis estadístico mostró que las zanjas de infiltración reducen significativamente la escorrentía. En promedio en los estudios anali- zados, las zanjas de infiltración redujeron la escorrentía en un 46.4%. En valores relativos esta reducción representa el 5.7% de la lluvia en promedio. (English: Among the eleven studies that measured runoff on 52 plots, all showed a reduction in runoff as a result of infiltration trenches. In relative values this reduction represents 5.7% of rainfall on average.)

Nesse nível de acesso, a distância percorrida não ultrapassa um quilômetro, o tempo gasto não ultrapassa 30 minutos e o volume médio coletado é de 20 litros per capita por dia18. EV_evidence_register.quote: Ocorre que, no entanto, mesmo com as cisternas, o carro-pipa continuou sendo uma realidade neces­ sária no semiárido e as pessoas continuam sujeitas à tentativa de uso político, porque a falta de água as coloca em uma situação muito vulnerável, como no caso das grandes secas plurianuais, explica a coordenadora local do MOC na Bahia: Então, imagina quando seca tudo. E a água da cis­ terna vai acabando. Como é que não dou um pote de água para meus bodes, minhas galinhas? Aí, o vereador chega lá e diz “não se preocupe, eu vou te dar um pipa”. Se, nesse momento, aquele vereador manda uma água para aquela família, ela vai ficar com um sentimento de gratidão [...]. Então, mas a água é um direito, e o direito não pode ser negociado. (Entrevista 5; Arsky 2019). (English: It happens, however, that even with the cisterns, the water truck continued to be a necessary reality in the semi-arid and people remain subject to attempts at political use, because the lack of water puts them in a very vulnerable situation, as in the case of the great multi-year droughts, explains the local MOC coordinator in Bahia: So, imagine when everything dries up. And the cistern water runs out. How can I not give a pot of water to my goats, my chickens? Then the councillor arrives and says 'don't worry, I'll give you a truckload'. If at that moment that councillor sends water to that family, she will feel gratitude [...]. But water is a right, and a right cannot be negotiated. (Interview 5; Arsky 2019).)

Foi muito fácil perceber, na observação direta da pesquisa de campo, como se apresentam as ca­ tegorias dignidade e autonomia. Resultado de um consistente processo de capacitação e conscien­ tização, existe hoje uma verdadeira cultura sobre o gerenciamento da água armazenada na cisterna, e a água de beber armazenada é tratada com zelo e cuidado. Essa reserva adicional, essa poupança, adia ou até mesmo evita as situações limites em que viviam essas famílias. (English: In addition, it conferred autonomy, because the benefiting family 'manages to go without depending on the water truck. It has independence, it has freedom, it doesn't have to sell its vote because of the water truck' (Interview 13; Arsky, 2019), explained the president of ARCAS (BA). It was very easy to perceive, in direct field observation, how the categories of dignity and autonomy present themselves. As a result of a consistent process of training and awareness-raising, there is today a true culture of managing the water stored in the cistern, and the stored drinking water is treated with zeal and care. This additional reserve, this saving, postpones or even avoids the extreme situations in which these families used to live.)

[...] Foi bom depois dessa água. Até agora mesmo, os tanques de barro estão secos e os animais estão se abastecendo da cisterna. A gente até parou de plantar um pouco, porque estamos poupando para os animais. [...] Se não fosse ela [a água estocada na cisterna] não dava. Porque a água da EMBASA [Empresa Baiana de Águas e Saneamento] não dá, porque passa da taxa. E, também, nós nem teríamos como armazenar, porque a água vem de oito em oito dias, e nós aqui em cima somos o último a receber, então quando chega nossa vez, já é hora de acabar de novo [...]. A água que tá na cisterna é da chuva e ainda tem como segurar alguns meses. (English: We had difficulty with water, because from where we live to the fields, to the tanks, it is quite far, and now not, because we got the cistern with a pump, and the extension comes with the project itself. [...] It was good after this water. Even right now, the clay tanks are dry and the animals are drinking from the cistern. We even stopped planting a bit, because we are saving it for the animals. [...] If it weren't for it [the water stored in the cistern] it wouldn't be possible. Because the EMBASA [Bahia water and sanitation company] water isn't enough, because it exceeds the fee. And also we wouldn't even have a way to store it, because the water comes every eight days, and up here we are the last to receive it, so when our turn comes it is already time for it to end again [...]. relationship.outcome_raw: cisterns (consumption + production) credited with a large reduction in rural establishments without any water source (census-based inference, no counterfactual)

context.note: IPEA review author's inference from Censo Agropecuario 2017 counts; mixes consumption (rooftop) and production cisterns, modal = rooftop consumption cisterns

EV_evidence_register.quote: De todo modo, das mais de 1 milhão de cisternas de consumo e produção construídas, a maio­ ria encontra-se no meio rural (tabela 4) e, nesse sentido, é inegável sua significativa contribuição para a ampliação do acesso à água na região. Considerando-se que em 2017 aproximadamente 446 mil estabelecimentos agropecuários no semiárido não possuíam acesso à nenhuma fonte hídrica,16 havendo um número de mais de 1 milhão de cisternas construídas, boa parte das quais no semiárido e no meio rural, é fácil concluir que o número de estabelecimentos, principalmente familiares (tabela 4), e, consequentemente, pessoas sem acesso à água seria muito maior. Esses dados confirmam que, justamente onde esperado, no meio rural, as cisternas contribuem de modo evidente, com a consecução da meta 6.1 do ODS da água. (English: In any case, of the more than 1 million consumption and production cisterns built, most are in rural areas (table 4) and, in this sense, their significant contribution to expanding access to water in the region is undeniable. Considering that in 2017 approximately 446 thousand agricultural establishments in the semi-arid had no access to any water source,16 with more than 1 million cisterns built, a good part of them in the semi-arid and in rural areas, it is easy to conclude that the number of establishments, mainly family farms (table 4), and consequently of people without access to water would be much greater. These data confirm that, exactly where expected, in rural areas, cisterns contribute clearly to achieving SDG target 6.1 on water.)

EV_evidence_register.quote: A barragem subterrânea de maior porte, como as construídas na região de Mutuca, pode proporcionar projetos de pequena irrigação e gerar renda direta e indireta para os proprietários da terra e a comunidade.
